title: Rendering lard from home pigs
subtitle: Turning back fat and leaf fat into clean, stable cooking fat.
excerpt: Lard from a home pig is a different product from commercial hydrogenated fat: white, firm, and clean-flavoured from leaf fat, softer and more distinctively porky from back fat. Rendering is a simple process of slow melting, straining, and chilling. A 20 kg pig yields roughly 1.5 to 2 kg of lard from the back fat alone.
sourceNotes: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Composition of Foods (1963), pork fat tables. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (9th edn., 1994), pork butchery chapter. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, chapter on pork lard.

glossaryTerms.definition: The soft, flaky fat surrounding the kidneys inside the abdominal cavity. Produces the mildest, whitest lard.
The solid residue left after the fat has melted out of the tissue during rendering. Salted and dried, they are edible.

content.text: Lard is pig fat rendered slowly until the tissue releases its stored fat, which is then strained and poured into jars.
from around the kidneys gives the palest, most neutral result. Back fat gives a soft lard with a mild pork flavour. Both keep for 6 to 12 months in a cool larder.
Work with cold fat straight from the refrigerator. Warm fat is slippery and harder to cut cleanly.

Trim away any blood-stained pieces, glands, or skin. These will taint the flavour. Cut the remaining fat into roughly 2 cm cubes. Smaller pieces render faster; larger pieces can scorch on the outside before the inside melts.
Add 150 ml of water to a heavy-bottomed stockpot before adding the fat. The water prevents the fat from scorching during the early stage before the fat is liquid enough to protect itself.

Heat the pot over the lowest flame your hob allows. The fat should melt slowly over 1 to 2 hours, never reaching a full simmer. A rolling boil scorches the lard and produces a dark, strong-tasting result.
Stir every 15 to 20 minutes, scraping the bottom of the pot. The solid pieces will gradually shrink as the fat melts out of them.
The rendering is nearly complete when the pieces stop shrinking and begin to look golden and slightly crisp. The liquid fat should be pale yellow and clear. Remove from heat before the pieces brown.
Line a sieve with two layers of muslin cloth. Set it over a large bowl or clean stockpot.
Ladle the hot fat carefully through the sieve. Work in batches to avoid overflow. The liquid fat runs through clear; the fibrous residue collects in the cloth.

Pour the strained liquid lard into sterilised jam jars. Fill to within 1 cm of the top, seal with a lid, and leave to set at room temperature. The lard turns white and opaque as it cools. Refrigerate once opened.

left in the muslin after straining can be salted and spread on bread, or pressed while hot into small rounds and dried in a low oven (120 C for an hour) to make pork scratchings. Cool completely before storing.

attrs.cue: Lard is dark or has a strong pork smell
attrs.cause: Heat was too high, or skin or glands were left in the fat
attrs.fix: Use a lower setting and check the fat more carefully next time. Dark lard is still safe to use but suits savoury cooking only.

attrs.cue: Lard turns rancid within a few weeks
attrs.cause: Stored at room temperature or in a warm larder, or liquid water remained in the jar
attrs.fix: Ensure the rendered fat is entirely free of water before potting. Heat it a little longer until the water has evaporated (no bubbling in the pot). Store in a cool, dark larder or the refrigerator.
